mercy_translation.text:
I praised the love of learning and the willingness to labor that mark your character, and I was extraordinarily pleased by the careful and sober attention of your mind, through which you think that no expression used about God in any ordinary form of theological speech ought to be left unexamined, my dear and most precious brother Amphilochius. For you have rightly heard the Lord’s exhortation that “everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds,” and by your diligence in asking you seem able to stir even the most reluctant person to share what he knows.

I admire still more that you put questions not, as many do today, merely to test us, but in order to discover what is actually true. There are plenty of people now who listen in order to catch us out and question us for controversy; but it is very difficult to meet a soul genuinely eager to learn, searching for truth because it recognizes its own ignorance. Like a hunter’s snare or an ambush in war, the questions of many people conceal a carefully prepared trap: they put forward arguments not so that they may gain something useful from them, but so that, if the answers do not agree with what they want, they may think they have found a just pretext for conflict.

If even a foolish person who asks a question may sometimes be credited with wisdom, how highly should we value an intelligent hearer—the one whom the prophet places beside the Wonderful Counselor? Such a hearer deserves every approval. It is right to advance with him, to accompany his earnestness, and to share the labor of his progress toward perfection.

Not to listen carelessly to theological expressions, but to try to trace the meaning hidden in every word and every syllable, is not the work of people idle in devotion, but of those who understand the purpose of our calling: that, as far as human nature is capable, we are set toward likeness to God. Likeness is not attained without knowledge, and knowledge does not arise apart from teaching. Speech is the beginning of teaching, and syllables and words are the parts of speech. Therefore examination of syllables is not outside our purpose.

Nor should questions be ignored merely because they seem small. Because truth is difficult to hunt down, we must trace it from every side. If, as in the arts, growth in true religion comes through additions made little by little, then those being introduced to knowledge must despise nothing. Someone who overlooks the first elements because they seem small will never attain the perfection of wisdom.

“Yes” and “no” are only two short expressions, yet the greatest good, truth, and the furthest boundary of evil, falsehood, are often contained in these little words. Why mention only this? There have even been cases in testimony for Christ where a mere nod of the head was judged to amount to a complete confession or denial of religion. If this is so, what theological expression can be so small that, whether used rightly or wrongly, it does not exert a great influence in one direction or the other? If not one iota or one stroke of the Law will pass away, how could it be safe for us to pass over even the smallest matters?

The expressions you asked us to distinguish are therefore both small and great: small because they are brief when spoken and perhaps for that reason easily despised, but great because of the force of what they signify. They are like the mustard seed: the smallest of seeds, yet, when it receives the proper care, it rises to considerable height as the power hidden within it unfolds.

If anyone laughs at what, to use the language of the Psalm, may look like our long discourse about syllables, let him reap the useless fruit of his laughter. We, however, should not surrender to human reproaches or abandon the investigation because others belittle it. I am so far from being ashamed of these matters as trivial that, if I could reach even a very small part of their true worth, I would congratulate myself as having obtained something great, and I would say that the brother who investigates these things with us has carried away no small profit.

Seeing, then, that a very great contest lies within very small expressions, I do not shrink from the labor because of the hope of reward. I believe the discussion will bear fruit for me and bring enduring benefit to those who hear it. Therefore, with the Holy Spirit himself, so to speak, I will now proceed to the explanation. And, if you wish me to set the discussion upon its proper road, I will first turn briefly back to the origin of the question.

Recently, while I was praying with the people and completing the doxology to God the Father in two forms—at one time saying “with the Son together with the Holy Spirit,” and at another “through the Son in the Holy Spirit”—some of those present objected that we were using unfamiliar expressions and, moreover, expressions they claimed were mutually inconsistent.

You therefore asked, primarily for their own benefit—or, if they are altogether incurable, at least for the safety of those who encounter them—that a clear teaching be set forth concerning the force of these expressions. We must therefore speak briefly, as far as possible, by first laying down a starting point acknowledged by the argument.

translator_notes: Translated directly from Basil's Greek, not from a modern English translation.
Basil addresses Amphilochius of Iconium and explains that the treatise arose from controversy over two forms of the doxology.
The chapter's insistence on words and syllables is methodological: small grammatical choices can carry major doctrinal implications.
The Greek source for this first unit is normalized from PG 32 and remains marked for philological review against the printed columns.
